result:
There is a specific, quiet magic to the concept of "deep time." 

Human beings are notoriously terrible at grasping the truly abstract. We understand a lifespan of eighty years because we can feel it—the seasons cycling, the slow turning of hair to silver, the stretch and snap of memory. We can even somewhat comprehend a few centuries, framing them through the rise and fall of empires or the dusty pages of recorded history. 

But when we try to look further, our minds hit a wall. 

I love standing in a canyon or hiking on a mountain trail and letting my brain attempt—inevitably failing, but trying—to comprehend the sheer, staggering weight of geological time. I’ll press my hand against a slab of grey limestone or red sandstone and think about what it used to be. 

That rock wasn't always rock. Millions upon millions of years ago, it was the bottom of a sprawling, ancient ocean. It was crushed shells of microscopic creatures. It was sediment carried down by rivers from mountains that have since entirely eroded into dust. The ground I am standing on was once the sky of a completely different world, buried under miles of ice, or part of a supercontinent tearing itself apart.

And before the rock? The atoms that make up the stone, the dirt, the trees, and me were forged in the collapsing hearts of dying stars, lightyears away. We are, quite literally, the leftover debris of cosmic explosions, briefly organized into the shapes of mountains, rivers, and human beings.

There is something profoundly comforting in this insignificance. 

We spend so much of our brief, bright lives agonizing over mistakes, stressing over the future, and desperately trying to leave a legacy. We want to carve our names into the bark of the universe and say, *I was here! Remember me!*

But standing against the backdrop of deep time, the pressure to be perfect dissolves. We are not meant to last forever. We are just a fleeting, spectacular weather pattern on the skin of the Earth. A brief, beautiful condensation of stardust that gets to walk around, drink coffee, listen to music, and feel the sun on its face for a few decades.

When the Earth eventually swallows our cities back into the soil, and millions of years turn our plastic and concrete into strange, new strata in the rock, the planet will simply breathe out and keep going. 

We are given a tiny, miraculous window to exist. To be the universe looking back at itself, if only for a moment. Realizing how small we are doesn't have to be scary; it can be the ultimate freedom. If nothing we do lasts forever, then the only thing that matters is the kindness we share, the art we make, and the quiet joy we take in being here, right now, before we return to the dust.
